segments.narration: Twenty-six metres down off Japan sits a stone staircase. Yonaguni, the far western tip of the Ryukyu Islands. A diver found it in 1986.
Flat terraces. Right angles. Walls that look cut. Kihachiro Aratake was out looking for hammerhead sharks when he swam into the thing.
A Ryukyu University geologist, Masaaki Kimura, called it a sunken city. Pyramids, roads, a stadium. Was there a lost civilisation under Japan?
Other geologists dived it and found the answer in the rock itself. Sandstone, about twenty million years old, sliced through by parallel bedding planes and vertical fractures.
Water prises those seams apart into steps and clean corners. And in forty years nobody has found a tool mark, a carving or a single artifact down there.

verdicts.claim: The Yonaguni formation lies about 26 metres deep off Yonaguni Island in Japan's Ryukyu Islands and was noticed in 1986.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: about 26 m (85 ft) deep below Arakawabana cliff, noticed in 1986.

verdicts.claim: The formation is Early Miocene sandstone and mudstone roughly 20 million years old, cut by parallel bedding planes and vertical joints.
verdicts.note: 87% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Geologists including Robert Schoch attribute the steps and right angles to erosion along those seams, and no artifacts or tool marks have been found at the site.
verdicts.note: Schoch, Wichmann and Ogata et al. (2019) all attribute the features to weathering and erosion; no artifacts are reported, and a 2024 Kyushu University survey found no traces of human activity. The narration's 'forty years' counts from the 1986 discovery.
